MJ Vigeant, owner of All-Ways Travels was looking for a career change when her daughter Tanya Slack who already worked at the agency, encouraged her to buy the business. Vigeant purchased it in Nov. 2017. When the COVID-19 pandemic brought the travel industry to a standstill, Williams Lake residents still had places they needed to go. For MJ Vigeant, keeping All-Ways Travel open meant helping people make essential journeys that couldn’t wait. Vigeant and her daughter, manager Tanya Slack, recalled how travel restrictions interrupted their growth plans and left the agency unable to keep staff on. Vigeant continued working through the uncertainty. “I’ve never had so many tears”, said Vigeant, recalling her work helping residents reach immediate family members abroad. That commitment to personal service is part of the story behind All-Ways Travel, which received the top honours award of the night, “Ken Wilson Chamber Business of the Year (Judge’s Choice Awards) at the Williams Lake & District Chamber of Commerce Business Excellence Awards on Oct. 24. The Ken Wilson Chamber Business of the Year (Judge’s Choice Awards recognize leadership, business performance, and commitment to the Chamber and local business community. It is selected by judges from nominated Chamber member businesses. Established in 1978, All-Ways Travel entered a new chapter when Vigeant purchased the agency in Nov. 2017. Her daughter, Slack, was already working there when her mother began considering a career change. The purchase brought them together in a business centred on helping people navigate travel. 6d2c9ebe724f840d1107378ac458f50a.text: The Williams Lake Mustangs extended their winning streak to 11 games with a 7-1 victory over the Summerland Jets at home on Sunday, Nov. 8. The Williams Lake earned their 10th straight win with a 4-0 shutout over the Beaver Valley Nitehawks at home on Saturday, Nov. 7. The Williams Lake Mustangs sit atop the BCHC standings with 31 points after extending their winning streak to 11 games over the weekend. The Williams Lake Mustangs skate a lap of the ice and tap their sticks to thank spectators following their 7-1 home win over the Summerland Jets on Sunday, Nov. 8. The Williams Lake Mustangs lost some hair but kept their winning streak after earning their 10th straight win with a 4-0 shutout over Beaver Valley Nitehawks at home on Saturday, Nov. 7 fulfilling a deal with their coach. Tristan Aidoo rounded out the scoring, assisted by Hauk and Blake Collison. Mustangs goaltender Ivan Anderson stopped all 41 shots he faced to earn the shutout and first star honours. 23cbdebac018ea0ef9f9e89d1aedd9c4.text: Mother testifies at inquest into police shooting death of B.C. teen | Williams Lake Tribune Mother testifies at inquest into police shooting death of B.C. teen An inquest into the shooting death of Chase De Balinhard began Nov. 9. An inquest to examine the circumstances surrounding the death of Surrey teen Chase de Balinhard, who was fatally shot by police in February 2025, began Nov. 9 in Burnaby. The inquest follows a December 2025 report by the Independent Investigations Office (IIO)—B.C.’s police watchdog—that found the two officers who opened fire on the autistic teen were legally justified. Separate from the IIO investigation, the inquest does not look at criminal or civil liability in Chase’s death. During the inquest, a jury will look at the evidence surrounding Chase’s death and make recommendations in an effort to prevent similar incidents in the future. Chase, who lived with autism and ADHD, left his home Feb. 9, 2025, with a pellet handgun. Within minutes, the 15-year-old Clayton teen called 911. Chase was shot by police a short time later. “Let’s have something good come from this, please!” implored Chase’s mom, Crystal de Balinhard, as she gave testimony first at the inquest. Crystal—at times tear-laden, scattered, and overcome by the emotion of the moment—advocated for more training for frontline workers dealing with kids and young adults who are on the autism spectrum. She recounted the events that led up to Chase’s death. Chase had become “dysregulated” or shutdown, meaning he was having a hard time managing his emotions and responses to others. Crystal said she heard there was a shooting in the area and she pinged Chase’s phone, but didn’t hear anything back. She searched his phone on a location app and it was showing in two spots, both near where the shooting was supposed to have taken place. She said Chase was always filming things and she thought he was up there filming. So, she sped to the intersection. She tried to get near the corner of 70th

1e4cd4706cd83e2784f8a102b51044f9.text: Millar Western announced indefinite curtailment of Quesnel River Pulp. Millar Western Forest Products Ltd. will indefinitely curtail operations at its Quesnel River Pulp mill, citing market conditions and uncertainty surrounding economic fibre supply. The *Quesnel Cariboo Observer* obtained a copy of a letter sent out on Nov. 9, to employees at the Quesnel River Pulp mill. In the letter, executive chair and CEO Karl Meyers said the company had made the “very difficult decision” to curtail Quesnel River Pulp mill for an indefinite period. “Based on current contractual obligations, we will continue operating the effluent system for twelve months, or until we can reach an acceptable alternative,” Meyers said in the letter. “We will continue to complete an orderly shutdown of the balance of the operations over the next several weeks, setting it up for a potential restart in the future.” In August, Millar Western announced temporary curtailment of operations until at least November. Meyers said the company reviewed all alternatives before concluding that an indefinite curtailment was the only viable option at this time. According to the letter, the duration of the curtailment remains unknown and will depend on market conditions and the availability of economic fibre supply. “As a result, we will be terminating employment for all those impacted and providing severance compensation and other support,” Meyers wrote. He added the company will also provide continuation of certain benefits and access to employee and family assistance resources, with details to be outlined in individual severance letters. Meyers said Millar Western will also look at filling vacancies at other company operations with displaced employees. “For those who will continue to work, the period between now and your final day of employment will be considered as working notice,” he said. According to the letter, to qualify for severance, employees must remain active until their last scheduled day of work.

eb246ae12ae1bc869b4fe0fba0a41106.text: Abbotsford's Sandeep Singh Kaila appears in the 2027 Guinness World Records book. There’s once again a little piece of Abbotsford in one of the world’s most popular books. A colour picture of Abbotsford’s Sandeep Singh Kaila’s legendary ball spinning exploits appears in the 2027 Guinness World Records book and this marks the third time in the past eight editions he has been featured with a photo. Kaila initially began making headlines in The Abbotsford News back in 2018 when he established a new time record of 60.5 seconds for spinning a basketball on a toothbrush. That record eventually was certified by the Guinness World Records group and a picture of him doing that activity was found on the 2019 book cover. Kaila was the first person ever to spin a basketball on a toothbrush for more than a minute. However, he sought more and began branching out to more ball spinning skills. He set a new mark for spinning a football on one finger in 2021, followed that up with another record set by spinning a rugby ball on one finger and then set another in 2024 by spinning two footballs at once. Kaila went on to establish new records in all three aforementioned categories in 2024 and has held them ever since. Two footballs is 21.23 seconds (July 4, 2024 in Abbotsford), rugby is 40.95 seconds (Nov. 13, 2024 in Abbotsford) and one football on a finger is 40.56 seconds (March 8, 2024 in Abbotsford). He said being acknowledged in the book is the culmination of years of hard work. “Being featured in the Guinness World Records book is one of the proudest moments of my life,” he said. “It represents years of dedication and practice. When I started spinning balls it was simply a passion I developed through my love of sports. I never imagined to be published in one of the world’s most famous books.” Kaila said he hopes his efforts can inspire others to follow his path. ab8f176b2c6fb9cd796290586d2c28d8.text: Kelowna MP Stephen Fuhr speaking about Canada's 2027 budget to reporters in front of the Pleasantvale II affordable housing building in Kelowna, B.C. on Sunday, Nov. 8. The Federal government’s plan to “end homelessness” within 10 years could have impact in Kelowna. On Nov. 5, the federal government tabled its 2027 budget, which includes almost $30 billion dedicated to the goal of eliminating homelessness within the next decade, as well as $15 billion to triple the number of annual non-market housing starts to 24,000. “Canadians always care for each other. The crisis of homelessness that has deepened since the pandemic strikes at the heart of Canadian values of fairness, solidarity, and human dignity,” the federal government said in its announcement of the 2027 budget. In Kelowna, MP Stephen Fuhr – also the Secretary of State for Defence Procurement – spoke about the budget to reporters and constituents at the Pleasantvale II apartment building, a subsidized housing project containing of mix of market and non-market units that is being lived in by many who were evacuated from UBC Okanagan’s Hadgraft Wilson building. “Housing is an issue. It’s becoming more unaffordable, not less, so we’re going to have to do a lot more.” Fuhr said the Pleasantvale II building was realized with a mix of federal, provincial and municipal government support, as well the affordable housing organization, the Society of Hope. The building represents a similar project to what the newly announced funding can produce. He said communities can apply to the federal government for funding, and added that is something Kelowna city staff excel at. “Kelowna always meets the terms and conditions, gets projects out of the ground and they do it quickly,” Fuhr said. “I think our level of commitment is indicated in the budget, and we’re going to do everything that we can to work with our partners.” He said the $45 billion budgeted to address homelessness is “aggressive, but it’s necessary,” adding that

c63787ba576e9f338793e2d39e0a32e8.text: Penticton's Courthouse hears both provincial and supreme court cases. **WARNING: This article contains details about a criminal sexual assault trial and may be disturbing to some readers. If you or someone you know has been impacted by sexual violence, contact the 24-hour Sexual Assault Support Crisis line at 1-877-954-6242 or the RCMP.** A former Indigenous spiritual healer banned from all Okanagan band territories will be back in court as the Syilx Okanagan Nation Alliance blasts his “self-serving” appeal. Donald Wayne Ashley was convicted of simple assault following a jury trial in 2024 over charges of sexually assaulting six different women during healing sessions in their homes on Penticton Indian Band Land over four days in 2022. One charge was stayed at the start of the trial, and two more charges were dropped during the month-long trial, according to the direction by the presiding Justice. Jury deliberations took almost three days, and at the end, the only crime the jurors found Ashley to be guilty of beyond a reasonable doubt was common assault of the first survivor to testify. The ONA announced in 2025, in a joint statement from Chiefs of all the member nations, that they collectively condemned Ashley’s actions and the Canadian legal system that they said failed in protecting their community, and called out the provincial and federal governments for failing to uphold their obligations as laid out by the National Inquiry in Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls. Sentenced later that year, as reported by IndigiNews, Ashley did not receive any jail time, but a two-year probation order with a one-year ban on offering healing sessions. In a release issued on Nov. 9, four days ahead of Ashley’s scheduled appearance in the Court of Appeal in Kelowna, the ONA blasted Ashley for once again forcing the survivors and their families to have their experiences dragged back through court. “The Syilx Okanagan Nation stands resolutely behind our women survivors

d64220e0d9d392402c66da7bf8404565.text: On Nov. 3, 2026, a semi-truck went into a ditch a few kilometres north of Vavenby. An RCMP sergeant shared some thoughts on highway safety after a semi-truck wound up in a ditch early Tuesday morning north of Vavenby. According to Sgt. Grant Simpson of the Clearwater RCMP, the driver reported the incident after it occurred on Highway 5 around 4:55 a.m. on Nov. 3. “Evidence at the scene suggests that the driver simply failed to negotiate the corner, likely due to speed or fatigue (despite having a relief driver on board as well) or a combination of both,” Simpson said. “Neither driver was injured and damage to the tractor and trailer was minimal.” The incident occurred roughly four or five kilometres north of Vavenby on Highway 5. At around 11 a.m. on Nov. 4, towing crews worked to remove the truck and traffic was reduced to one lane for a short stretch of highway. Simpson said no charges were laid as a result of the incident. He explained police did not know his speed, nor did the driver admit to falling asleep or being tired. The sergeant noted a language barrier that made communication difficult, and added that the driver said he swerved to avoid an animal. “But there’s no evidence of that there. The evidence is clear that he just drove, like he just wasn’t able to make the corner. It was a left-hand corner, fairly sharp. Not anything that you couldn’t manage unless you were going too fast.” Simpson said he’s been in contact with the related trucking company multiple times to discuss his concerns “regarding the safety of our highways and other motorists sharing the roads” with its drivers. The sergeant did not share the name of the company for privacy reasons. Simpson, who said he was once a professional driver, shared some thoughts about truckers and highway safety. “Their time is always a big concern. They’re always in a hurry to get to their location. A prayer at the newly renovated public library in Williams Lake was provided by Williams Lake First Nation elder Virginia Gilbert who was joined with Frances Supernault for drumming and singing. Attending the grand reopening of the Williams Lake public library on Tuesday, Nov. 10 was Williams Lake Mayor Surinderpal Rathor who was joined with councillors Nathan Wiebe, Paul French and Ruth Lloyd. Cariboo Regional District (CRD) chair and Electoral Area H Director Margo Wagner. A fresh new look at the Cariboo Regional District Library in Williams Lake was recently celebrated following two months of renovations. The branch was temporarily closed in September and October with limited services available through outdoor pop-up libraries to allow for repainting in addition to new carpeting, furnishings and circulation desk. It reopened on Tuesday, Nov. 3 with a grand reopening a week later that included Virginia Gilbert and Frances Supernault of the Williams Lake First Nation providing a prayer, drumming and singing. Speeches were additionally shared by officials including Cariboo Regional District (CRD) chair and Electoral Area H Director Margo Wagner and Williams Lake Mayor Surinderpal Rathor. Wagner admitted she is not in the library often although she does access electronic materials. “But the difference from when I was here last time is unbelievable,” she said. “It’s so much brighter, there seems to be more room, there’s more additions that make it more like a living room rather than a library.” Funding for the project was provided by the BC Public Library Enhancement Grant that Manager of Library Services Jennifer Coupe said they had received in 2023. “It took three and half years to get this project off the ground and it was well worth it,” she said, thanking staff for their countless

The cenotaph was re-dedicated in front of city hall on Nov. 3, 1984. From spectators gathering for a flag-raising at a new Cenotaph in 1968 to veterans marching to city hall for a Korean War plaque dedication in 1994, Williams Lake has a long tradition of honouring those who served – one that continues. The Williams Lake and District Cenotaph was built in 1968 below the former War Memorial Hospital, a joint undertaking by the municipality and Royal Canadian Legion Branch 139 to honour the area’s war dead, according to the Veterans Affairs Canada’s website. The Cariboo War Memorial Hospital opened in May 1925, partly funded by the community of Soda Creek to honour fallen First World War soldiers. In 1968, the _Williams Lake Tribune_ reported on spectators gathering for a flag-raising ceremony at the new monument. Sixteen years later, the cenotaph was moved beside city hall and rededicated on Nov. 3, 1984, in conjunction with the dedication of the new municipal building. Days after the cenotaph’s rededication beside city hall, the _Tribune’s_ Nov. 8, 1984 edition outlined the plans for that year’s Remembrance Day Observance, bringing together veterans, students and community groups. The service began at 10:45 a.m. at the Elks Hall on Nov. 11, 1984 with the Williams Lake Community Band playing O Canada and a student from Anne Stevenson Junior Secondary School’s drama class reading In Flanders Field. Bill Lannigan and A.E McMath read the names of the former residents who died in the First and Second World Wars, followed by the Last Post and two minutes of silence. After the service, Legion members, RCMP, Sea Cadets, Air Cadets and youth organizations included Cubs, Scouts, Voyageurs, Guides and Brownies paraded to the cenotaph for wreath-laying, before returning to the Legion hall to lay wreaths at its cairn. e77d4e4cbc4c3b21610adcc1b8f5786c.text: Cariboo-Prince George-Omineca MP Todd Doherty is critical of the 2026 federal budget. On Thursday, Nov. 5, Prime Minister Mark Carney presented the 2026 federal budget in Parliament. In this extensive budget, Carney has outlined a plan to invest more in the economy and culture of Canada to help address the affordability crisis and the general economic uncertainty gripping the global economy. The budget also calls for constructing more affordable housing and accommodations for the 65,000 Canadians experiencing homelessness. “Investment that builds our sovereignty. Entrepreneurs empowered to grow. Ideas that become companies. Artists who tell our stories. Energy we generate and control. More choices and lower costs for you. A home for every Canadian,” Carney wrote in the budget’s cover letter. “This is what it means to be ‘Maîtres chez nous’. A sovereign Canada, where we take care of each other, where we create opportunities for all, and where we are free to live our lives as we choose.” A member of the Conservative Party, Doherty is critical of the Liberal Government’s budget, pointing specifically to the $765 billion in debt he said it will add to the country’s deficit over the next five years. Doherty said this is the equivalent of $44,000 in debt for every Canadian household. During a time when many Canadians are struggling to pay for groceries, fuel and housing, Doherty believes the country cannot afford a government that spends billions of dollars. He asserted the first goal of this budget should have been saving Canadians money, not putting more debt on their backs. “The fastest-growing item in this budget is interest on the national debt. By 2031, the federal government will be spending $17 billion more on debt interest than on healthcare transfers to provinces and territories,” Doherty said. “This is unacceptable.” While critical of the budget, Doherty noted there are investments in the budget that could benefit communities across his riding. The Regional District of North Okanagan is working with a local environmental group to assess what can be done about the pond. The City of Vernon’s new council held its first meeting Tuesday, and one of its first orders of business was to receive some worrisome information relating to the area’s water shortages heading into next year. Hayley Dosser, a scientist with the Canadian Centre for Climate Services, made a delegation to Vernon council at its inaugural meeting Nov. 10, to discuss what is expected to be the most intense super El Niño on record, which has been building in the tropical Pacific Ocean since September. An El Niño is a climate pattern that sees higher than average sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean create a shift in weather patterns well beyond the Pacific Ocean. A super El Niño is simply an extreme version of this phenomenon. Dosser said the temperature at the ocean’s surface has now passed three degrees Celsius above the baseline, “so we are in a very strong El Niño.” The climate scientist explained that this sets the stage for extreme weather and related impacts, such as were scene in the winters of 1982-83, 1997-98 and 2015-16. While the impacts of an El Niño are generally less severe in Canada compared to other countries, past events are estimated to have cost Canada billions of dollars, Dosser said. “This particular El Niño event is quite exceptional. It is very likely to be unprecedented, potentially by a substantial margin,” she added. In Canada, the strongest direct effects of El Niño on weather tend to occur in winter and spring, Dosser said. “We can see that we tend to have milder and drier winters with less snow. We also tend to have warmer, drier springs.” That should sound some alarm bells, as the North Okanagan’s snowpack and its spring precipitation levels have been described by the local water utility as variables that will decide

ae26be1308a32457a0321b8f732a9c40.text: B.C. businesswoman receives US$5K NEXUS fine in crackdown | Williams Lake Tribune South Surrey businesswoman Suzanne Smith says she is fighting the recent revocation of her NEXUS pass, as well as the US$5,000 fine she was handed. Suzanne Smith received confirmation of her NEXUS pass revocation in September. A South Surrey woman who operated three boutique stores south of the border for more than a dozen years before closing her last U.S. shop in May says she has been stripped of her trusted-traveller privileges and hit with a US$5,000 fine for violating a rule she never knew existed. Suzanne Smith of Betty Be Good Boutique said Nov. 2 that her experience has made her nervous about future crossings, and that it is a cautionary tale that she hopes others can learn from. “I’m someone who regularly crosses the border who did not know the rules of the game have changed,” said Smith. “I don’t want this to happen to other people, and I also want others to just be on alert if they’re planning to go there.” The incident that triggered the penalties occurred in September, when Smith used her NEXUS pass to cross the border to pick up business and personal parcels from her U.S. post-office box. Driving an empty vehicle, she said she “told the agent exactly why I was going down there, to pick up parcels,” and was waved through without further questions. Heading back to Canada, she encountered a checkpoint in the commercial lane. The border officer asked, “How did you get to America today?” and upon learning it was via the NEXUS lane, peppered Smith with “rapid-fire” questions: did she have a transponder? Had she told the earlier border officer that she was crossing for work? Had she paid the single-crossing fee – currently US$22.10 – required of those crossing into the U.S. for commercial purposes? 8f05f13d0d3df218e6113228dd1bf573.text: The Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation in Alberta is suing British Columbia, the federal government, and BC Hydro for what it says are Treaty 8 rights violations related to several dams on the Peace River, including Site C, now known as the John Horgan Dam. “The Province and British Columbia Hydro built these hydroelectric projects without regard for the rights, culture and way of life of ACFN, which includes the exercise of its Treaty Rights,” the lawsuit, filed on Nov. 5 in B.C. Supreme Court, argues. B.C.’s Ministry of Attorney General declined to comment on the case because the government is in “caretaker mode” following the Oct. 24 election. The incoming government is not due to be sworn in until Nov. 20. The First Nation signed Treaty 8 in 1899, guaranteeing protection for the Chipewyan way of life in exchange for allowing settlement and development in the nation’s territories. When B.C. began building dams along the Peace River, including the W.A.C. Bennnet Dam (completed in 1967), the Peace Canyon Dam (completed in 1980), and finally the Site C Dam (finished in 2024), the nation says the province failed to consult on the impacts on the Peace River Delta. And B.C. is now in the early stages of “information-gathering” on another potential dam on the river at a place known as Site E near the Alberta border. The nation says that BC Hydro did not even speak of the downstream impacts during hearings related to the earlier dams, and did not include the delta area in the environmental assessment area for Site C, claiming there would be “no detectable effects” from Site C. But the Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation says it is experiencing lasting impacts from the dams. The nation blames the dams for altering the river’s natural flow and seasonal timing, impacting water quality and interfering with the area’s natural ecology, which affects fish, wildlife and vegetation. Highway Patrol issued 6,695 tickets during its “Drive Relative to Conditions” campaign in October. While that’s down slightly from the 2025 numbers, B.C. An officer was patrolling in wet snow and rain on Highway 97C when a dark F-350 pickup emerged from the fog. Police said the officer got a radar reading of 166 km/h in a 110 zone. The release says that after the truck was stopped, police records showed the truck had not been inspected for mechanical modifications and defects after a prior police notice and order in August. Highway patrol says the total fines, repairs and at least three years of high-risk driver premiums and escalating insurance, will bring the estimated total costs to over $4,000. B.C. dbbbd2364c5ffb918f0e7577302f052e.text: Four grizzly bears, like the one pictured here, have been euthanized after being conclusively linked to fatal attack in Bella Coola. Four bears have been euthanized after being conclusively linked to the killing of a mother and daughter from Bella Coola. ​At a press conference on Tuesday, Nov. 10, BC Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) Inspector Jeff Tyre confirmed that forensic testing determined that four grizzly bears captured by the BCCOS over the last several days were all actively involved in the attack. ​“Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analyzed and conclusively linked to a sow and three offspring,” Tyre said. ​Family members have identified the victims as Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, who failed to return after going for a walk on the Snooka West Trail on Nov. 1. They were killed in a grizzly bear attack less than a year after several school children and one adult were left with serious injuries. The inspector added that the bears have been dispatched to protect the public after consideration of all the evidence and analysis of provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines. “This was a heartbreaking event for the families, the Nuxalk Nation and the Bella Coola community,” Tyre said. “We hope the efforts of everyone who responded, along with these findings, bring some measure of closure. Our thoughts remain with everyone affected.” According to Tyre, the investigation also pointed to likely predatory behaviour, which he stressed is very rare. “We don’t know how it started, but we know how it ended,” he said. The BCCOS inspector added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the complex investigation over the past week, working in difficult terrain and weather, while carefully managing ongoing risk to the public and responders involved. The Cabot Revelstoke Mountain Lodge under construction at Revelstoke Mountain Resort on Sept. 16. Green fees have been announced for Revelstoke’s new luxury golf course set to open next summer, though only hotel guests may play for the first season. Bookings for staying and playing at Cabot Revelstoke starting July 2027 have opened, its team announced early this month. The inaugural season for the 18-hole course at Revelstoke Mountain Resort will run July 2 to Sept. 30, but exclusively for golfers staying at the new 155-room Karl Hotel that overlooks the 18th green. For both local and visiting golfers interested in stays, “we’re delighted to extend an exclusive invitation to be among the first to experience this extraordinary destination, with priority access to golf stay-and-play reservations ahead of our broader public launch,” real estate manager Holly Nichols shared on Wednesday, Nov. 4. Golf rates for next year are $315 per round for non-local hotel guests, $225 for local hotel guests, $175 for junior hotel guests age 16 and under, and $175 for PGA members. To stay at the Karl Hotel, standard king rooms (the cheapest accommodation) fit two guests and cost $319. A standard double-queen room with two beds sleeps four guests and costs $399, making it the most affordable per-person option. These rates are subject to taxes and add-ons include sofa beds, balconies and kitchenettes. “Day golf” for players other than hotel guests is not currently available and will be added as an option at a later date, Cabot Revelstoke clarified. For now, Karl Hotel guests who submit a booking request can expect a follow-up from Cabot Revelstoke’s reservations team to confirm availability for stays and golf play. eae930c57c2abf322ad976158a7614e2.text: Prince George RCMP are asking for the public’s help to locate a young child who was reportedly seen running alone along the John Hart Bridge. According to an RCMP press release, police received multiple reports shortly before 6 p.m. on Wednesday, Nov. 6, of an unidentified child running on the roadway near the on-ramp from North Nechako Road to Highway 97 southbound. Mounties said the child was described as female, approximately three to six years old, with purple hair and wearing a green shirt. According to the release, multiple officers immediately attended the area and conducted extensive patrols, including a drone search, but were unable to locate the child. “We believe that the child may have been picked up by a guardian, who has decided not to report the situation,” Sgt. Craig Douglass of the Prince George RCMP said. “We would like to ask the guardian or anyone who knows this child to reach out to us so that we may confirm their well-being.” Police are also asking anyone with additional information or dashcam footage from the area at the time of the incident to come forward. Anyone with information or video footage is asked to contact the Prince George RCMP at 250-561-3300 as soon as possible.
